title: Room server
description: The room server's figures: who is playing, how it runs for them, and the server's own health.

panels.title: Players by platform
panels.description: Players seated in a room right now, by the platform their hello named. iPadOS Safari sends a Macintosh user agent, so iPads count as web, not web_ios. unknown is a client too old to name one.

panels.title: Rooms by kind and state
panels.description: Rooms held right now. waiting: one player and no partner yet; playing: two; interrupted: a partner the room already had is gone; empty: nobody, kept up to six minutes for a return. Empty rooms count against MAX_ROOMS too.

panels.title: Connections against the limit
panels.description: Open connections, seated or still saying hello, against the most the server holds at once (two per room at MAX_ROOMS plus sixty-four).

panels.title: Rooms against the limit
panels.description: Rooms of every state against MAX_ROOMS. Past the limit newcomers see SERVER IS BUSY.

panels.title: Page loads
panels.description: Over the dashboard's time range. The server counts events, not people: one person who reloads the page counts twice. Successful responses for the page itself. An uptime monitor pointed at / instead of /health inflates this.

panels.title: Engine downloads
panels.description: Over the dashboard's time range. The server counts events, not people: one person who reloads the page counts twice. Successful responses for the engine, gzipped or not. HEAD and partial (206) responses count as successful too. A browser with the engine cached asks and gets a 304, which is not counted here.

panels.title: Seatings by action
panels.description: Over the dashboard's time range. The server counts events, not people: one person who reloads the page counts twice. Players seated in a room: create opens a room by code, join enters one by code, quick is the quick game, return is coming back by code after a drop.

panels.title: Pairings
panels.description: Over the dashboard's time range. A pairing counts once per room, when both seats are first filled; a partner coming back afterward is not another pairing.

panels.title: Wait for a partner, p50 and p90
panels.description: How long the player already in a room waited for a partner who came, by kind of room. Over an hour rather than five minutes: pairings are rare next to packets. A code room's wait includes the time it took to pass the code on. Quantiles come from the buckets, never from sum over count: a mean is what a few slow connections drag furthest.

panels.title: Abandoned waits per hour
panels.description: Rooms swept with nobody having come to the player who waited, by kind. Observed when the empty room is swept, five to six minutes after it emptied; rooms still open at a restart are never observed.

panels.title: Pair-hours per day
panels.description: Hours two players spent in a room together over the last day, by kind: the time both seats were full, summed. Observed when the room is swept, five to six minutes late; a room still open at a restart is never observed.

panels.title: Players by version
panels.description: Players seated right now, by the version their hello named: the ten most common releases, other for the rest and anything that is not a release version, unknown for none. Live players only; while real traffic is low a handful of fake clients can rotate fake versions through the ten.

panels.title: Round trip to players, p50 and p95
panels.description: The server's own ping to each player and the pong back, by platform, about every twenty seconds a player. Godot answers a ping once a frame, so desktop and native figures include up to about 16 ms of the game loop; browsers answer at once. A client can make its own figure worse by answering late, never better. High RTT with a low worst gap is a slow but steady path, which the input delay absorbs. Quantiles come from the buckets, never from sum over count: a mean is what a few slow connections drag furthest.

panels.title: Server forward delay, p99
panels.description: From a packet read from a player to that packet in the partner's socket: the server's own delay, plus a partner's socket slow to take it. High here means the server itself: look at scheduler latency and CPU. A write that hits the five-second write limit is not observed: it becomes a disconnect or an eviction instead, and right after an eviction a burst of top-bucket observations is normal.

panels.title: Worst gap per window, p50 and p95
panels.description: The longest a player's stream of packets went quiet in each five-second window, as the server received it: jitter on the way to the server. It includes whole pauses in the middle of a connection too (menus, the STATS screen, a hidden tab), so read the upper quantiles, never a mean. A high worst gap with a normal RTT is jitter.

panels.title: Players' game speed, p10
panels.description: How fast players' games ran, as a share of full speed (sixty ticks a second), by platform: one player window in ten ran this slow or slower. A window in which the game stood frozen (a partner's hidden tab, a relay drop and return, the player's own hidden tab) is reported like any other: it reads as low speed with no waits, the machine verdict. Before blaming players' machines, check the worst gap, where a stand shows as a gap of seconds. Self-reported by the player's side: a client can forge these figures within the bounds the server clamps them to, and a handful of forgers can bend a distribution. Only network games played through this server report; single-player and LAN games are not measured.

panels.title: Windows by verdict
panels.description: Shares of reported windows: smooth at 95% of full speed or more; below that, network if the game waited for the partner's input, machine if it never did. Network: look at RTT and the worst gap. Machine: look at FPS for that platform, and at the worst gap, since the machine share includes frozen stands. A window in which the game stood frozen (a partner's hidden tab, a relay drop and return, the player's own hidden tab) is reported like any other: it reads as low speed with no waits, the machine verdict. Before blaming players' machines, check the worst gap, where a stand shows as a gap of seconds. Self-reported by the player's side: a client can forge these figures within the bounds the server clamps them to, and a handful of forgers can bend a distribution. Only network games played through this server report; single-player and LAN games are not measured.

panels.title: Input delay, p50 and p90
panels.description: The input delay players' games ran at, in ticks: five on a smooth link, up to sixteen on a ragged one. The delay grows when the network falls short of the round trip the match needs, and is carried between levels rather than reset at the start of each one. Self-reported by the player's side: a client can forge these figures within the bounds the server clamps them to, and a handful of forgers can bend a distribution. Only network games played through this server report; single-player and LAN games are not measured. Bucket bounds are whole numbers, which Prometheus 3 stores as 5.0: read them through quantiles, never by selecting a bound's text.

panels.title: Players' frame rate, p10
panels.description: Frames a second players' sides drew over a reported window, by platform: one window in ten drew this few or fewer. A window in which the game stood frozen (a partner's hidden tab, a relay drop and return, the player's own hidden tab) is reported like any other: it reads as low speed with no waits, the machine verdict. Before blaming players' machines, check the worst gap, where a stand shows as a gap of seconds. Self-reported by the player's side: a client can forge these figures within the bounds the server clamps them to, and a handful of forgers can bend a distribution. Only network games played through this server report; single-player and LAN games are not measured.

panels.title: Desynced matches
panels.description: Rooms whose two players' worlds parted, per hour, by kind: a bug in the game, not in the network. Counted once a room, only in a room that has held a pair. Self-reported by the player's side: a client can forge these figures within the bounds the server clamps them to, and a handful of forgers can bend a distribution. Only network games played through this server report; single-player and LAN games are not measured.

panels.title: Engine download time, p50 and p95
panels.description: How long a player waits for the engine to download, from the server starting on the request to the last byte handed to the connection. Over an hour: downloads are rare. A lower bound: socket and proxy buffers hide the rest, and behind nginx with proxy_buffering on it measures only the hop to the proxy. Quantiles come from the buckets, never from sum over count: a mean is what a few slow connections drag furthest.

panels.title: Go scheduler latency, p99
panels.description: How long goroutines that were ready to run waited for a CPU. Over ten milliseconds the process is starved of CPU, and every packet waits with it: check the machine's load and the container's CPU limit.

panels.title: GC pauses, p99
panels.description: How long the garbage collector stopped the whole process. Pauses stop packets as well.

panels.title: Refusals by reason
panels.description: Connections refused, per five minutes. rooms_limit and connections_limit both reach the player as SERVER IS BUSY; full is a code room with both seats taken; no_room a code that does not exist or has expired; bad_hello a first message the server could not read.

panels.title: Disconnects by cause
panels.description: Seated players' connections that ended, per five minutes. goodbye: they closed it, or the server did on a restart — a client answers the server's own close frame with one of its own; idle: silent past the read deadline; lost: dropped without a word; cut: ended by the server's side, which includes a peer whose write failed (a broken pipe or a reset), not only evictions; protocol: they broke the protocol.

panels.title: Evictions
panels.description: Players a room dropped per five minutes because their queue overflowed: their link took packets slower than the partner sent them.

panels.title: Rejected reports
panels.description: Players' reports dropped per five minutes. early: past the allowance (two at once, then one every four seconds) or a second desync; an honest client catching up can be early. malformed: neither of the two shapes, which is a client version writing the wrong shape or a script.

panels.title: Game file errors
panels.description: 4xx and 5xx responses for the game's files per five minutes, by route: page, wasm for the engine, other for the rest. A burst of 404s on other is usually a scanner.

panels.title: Journals capped
panels.description: Rooms whose journal reached its cap per five minutes: a player who drops after that cannot catch up.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: CPU the process used, in cores.

panels.title: Resident memory
panels.description: Memory the process holds. The deployment plan budgets about 400 MB at MAX_ROOMS=50.

panels.title: Open file descriptors
panels.description: Every connection is a descriptor, and a script opening sockets runs into the limit first.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: About two per seated player plus a few of the server's own.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Live heap after the last collection, and the size the collector lets it reach before the next.

panels.title: Journal bytes
panels.description: Memory every room's journal holds right now: the only thing in the server that grows with play.
